common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Decubitus Ulcer Sacral Myocutaneous Flap.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.

dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Decubitus Ulcer Sacral Myocutaneous Flap.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently assess for sepsis or spreading infection; obtain appropriate deep tissue or bone cultures when debridement is performed and use antibiotics guided by clinical findings and culture results. Maintain strict pressure off-loading, continence care, and nutritional optimization. Flap reconstruction should be planned by the specialist team only after the wound bed, infection control, and caregiver repositioning plan are adequate.

must_ask.say: How often is he turned or repositioned in bed?
How long has the sore been present, and has it gotten deeper?
Has he had any fevers or seemed more confused or unwell recently?
How has his appetite and weight been recently?
What is his baseline mobility since the stroke — can he shift his own weight?

history.answer: My father has a deep wound on his tailbone that won't heal, and the nursing home said it has gotten much worse.
He didn't suffer a cut or a fall; this sore developed simply from lying in bed constantly after his severe stroke.
A reddish spot appeared about three months ago, and over the past several weeks it broke open and grew much wider and deeper.
It is located directly over his tailbone and measures about three inches across, looking like a wide, deep crater.
The nursing home nurse told us last week that the sore is so deep you can actually see the whitish tailbone at the bottom.
There has been no exposure to dirt, rust, or animal bites, but it is very hard to keep his bowel movements from soiling the area.
We haven't seen any active spurting or heavy blood, just thick yellowish fluid with occasional streaks of blood on the gauze.
His feeling around that area is very poor, and he cannot move his legs properly because of his stroke.
He doesn't grimace or complain of much pain when they clean it, likely because he has lost so much sensation there.
The wound has been open for almost three months; they applied barrier creams, foam dressings, and saline gauze, but nothing healed it.
The skin around the hole is red, and it drains a foul-smelling yellowish pus that soaks through the bandages.
He has not had any shaking chills, body sweats, high fevers, or sudden worsening of his mental state.
He stays in bed around the clock; the staff are supposed to turn him every two hours, but with staffing shortages he often lies flat on his back much longer.
He lost control of both his bladder and bowels after the stroke, so he has to wear adult diapers continuously.
His appetite has been very poor for months, and he barely eats half of his meals, losing about ten pounds recently.
He suffered a major ischemic stroke two years ago that paralyzed his right side and took away his ability to walk or care for himself.
He has never had diabetes, and since he cannot walk at all, he hasn't had any calf cramping.
He has not received a tetanus shot in at least twenty or thirty years.
He does not take any steroid medications, chemotherapy, or immune-suppressing drugs.
There was absolutely no abuse, neglect from violence, or self-harm involved in this.
I think my backside broke open because the nursing home staff left me lying in one spot without turning me.
I'm terrified that this sore has gotten into my bone and will give me a fatal blood infection.
I'm hoping you can clean and bandage the sore properly and give me strong antibiotics so it can heal up.
He has high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, in addition to the severe stroke two years ago.
He was in the hospital for three weeks after his stroke two years ago, but he has never had any surgeries.
He takes lisinopril ten milligrams once a day for his blood pressure, and nothing else.
He does not have any known allergies to medications or latex.
He used to smoke a pack a day for twenty-five years, but he quit completely ten years ago.
He does not drink any alcohol and hasn't had a drink in decades.
He is a retired factory machinist and has lived in a specialized nursing facility for the past two years.
His father had hypertension and his mother passed away from a stroke in her seventies, but there are no other significant family illnesses.

exam.finding: Elderly bedbound male lying in lateral decubitus position, appearing frail and chronically ill with muscle wasting.
Blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert but minimally communicative with expressive dysphasia, following simple one-step commands.

An 8 cm by 7 cm full-thickness sacral defect with undermined edges, foul-smelling purulent exudate, and visible hard sacral bone with a positive probe-to-bone test, surrounded by 2 cm of periwound erythema without fluctuance.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with capillary refill under two seconds.
Markedly diminished light touch and pinprick sensation over the sacral region and bilateral lower extremities.
Right lower extremity shows flaccid paralysis with 0/5 motor strength and flexion contractures; left lower extremity shows 3/5 motor strength.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation with no wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended with normal active bowel sounds and no palpable masses.
